content: Cutaneous skin tags are small growths on the skin that are typically benign and harmless. These growths are often asymptomatic, with the only noticeable feature being the presence of the tag itself. They are usually small in size, though some may grow up to half an inch in length. Skin tags are commonly found on areas such as the neck, armpits, trunk, body folds, or other regions where skin rubs against skin. They may have a narrow stalk connecting them to the skin's surface and are usually the same color as the surrounding skin, though they can occasionally appear darker. The exact cause of cutaneous skin tags is not fully understood, but they are thought to result from friction caused by skin rubbing against itself. This is why they are more frequently observed in areas with skin folds. These growths are most common in individuals who are middle-aged or older, and they are more prevalent in people who are overweight or have diabetes. Skin tags are generally painless and do not grow or change over time, although they may become irritated if they are rubbed by clothing or other materials. The diagnosis of cutaneous skin tags is typically made based on their appearance. In rare cases, a biopsy may be performed to confirm the diagnosis if the growth has an unusual appearance. Medical attention should be sought if the appearance of a skin tag changes or if the patient wishes to have it removed for cosmetic or comfort reasons. Treatment for cutaneous skin tags is usually unnecessary unless they cause irritation or are considered cosmetically undesirable. When removal is desired, it can be achieved through surgical excision, freezing (cryotherapy), or cauterization (electrical burning). These procedures are generally effective, and the removed skin tags do not regrow. However, new skin tags may develop in other areas of the body over time. The prognosis for cutaneous skin tags is excellent, as they are benign and typically do not cause significant problems. While they may occasionally become irritated or bleed if cut, complications are rare. In some cases, individuals may find them cosmetically unappealing. After removal, there is usually no scarring, and the procedure is well-tolerated. In summary, cutaneous skin tags are common, benign skin growths that are generally harmless. They may be removed if they cause discomfort or cosmetic concerns, and the outcomes of treatment are typically favorable.
